question_en: An assumption of the binomial option pricing model is most likely:
option_a: the underlying can take on any value at the end of the period.
option_b: an option and its underlying can be used to create a hedged portfolio.
option_c: the actual probabilities of movements in the underlying are required by the model.
explanation_en: Assumptions of one-period binomial pricing model Underlying must increase or decrease each period. Underlying's end-of-period price is known today regardless of direction of movement. Volatility of underlying affects its end-of-period price. Option and underlying can be combined to create a perfectly hedged portfolio. Probability of underlying price increasing or decreasing each period is based on risk-neutral probability. The binomial option pricing model assumes that in each period the underlying price must move up or down, and that the two possible ending prices are known at the beginning of the period. The only unknown is the direction of the movement. This certainty allows construction of a portfolio that combines being long in some amount of the underlying with a short position in one European call option. The portfolio generates the same payoff (ie, hedged portfolio) at the end of the period regardless of whether the underlying price goes up or down. The formula to determine how much of the underlying to own is: Assume that a stock's price today is $20, and that in one year it will be either $24 or $16. This means that a European call option with a strike price of $20 that expires in one year will be worth either $4 or $0 at expiration, since the value of a call option is Maximum(Underlying price – Strike price). Recall that the strike price is zero. Inserting these numbers into the above formula shows that the quantity of stock to own is 0.5 shares: The value of the portfolio at the end of the period is $8 regardless of whether the underlying's price is $24 or $16: Underlying is $24 at the end of the period: ($24 × 0.5) − $4 = $8 Underlying is $16 at the end of the period: ($16 × 0.5) − $0 = $8 (Choice A) Since the binomial model allows the underlying's price to be only one of two possible values, it does not assume a random outcome. (Choice C) Probabilities of up and down moves are based on risk-neutral probabilities, not actual probabilities.

question_en: The current value of an option determined using a one-period binomial model is best described as its values in one period weighted by the:
option_b: probabilities of up and down moves discounted by the risk-free rate.
option_c: risk-neutral up and down probabilities discounted by the risk-free rate.
explanation_en: In binomial models, an option's value is the present value of the weighted average of its values in the up and down states, the two possible outcomes for each period forward in time. Starting from the current underlying asset price (S ), the asset's value will be either the underlying asset 0 price given an upward movement (S+) or a downward movement (S−). In one-period models, the length of a period is the time to expiration. S+, S−, and the option's strike price (X) are used to value the option's call price given either: an upward movement (c+), so that c+ = max(0, S+ − X), or a downward movement (c−), so that c− = max(0, S− − X). As with derivatives in general, binomial models assume arbitrage-free pricing holds for options, such that risk-free hedging strategies can be created. This affects both the weighting and discount rate used in determining option values: Risk-neutral probabilities are used to weight the option values in the up and down states. The risk-free rate is the appropriate discount rate since riskless positions should earn a risk-free rate of return. (Choice A) Risk-neutral probabilities are used to find the weighted average of the option values one period in the future, but that value must be discounted to obtain a present value. (Choice B) Probabilities of the up or down movements are not used in the binomial model and are not the same as risk-neutral probabilities.

subtopic: 8.10 Valuing a Derivative Using a One-Period Binomial Model
question_en: Which of the following assumptions is least likely to be valid when pricing options using the binomial pricing model?
option_a: Option prices are premised on investors being risk averse.
option_b: Actual probability of the underlying's up and down moves is unknown.
option_c: Volatility of the underlying determines the underlying's up and down moves.
explanation_en: The binomial option pricing model assumes that in any single period, the underlying must move up or down and that its price at the end of the period is known today in either case. The only unknown is the direction of the movement. For example, if today's price for a share of stock is $20, and the price during the year can either rise or fall by 20%, then its price at the end of the year is either $24 or $16; there are no other possibilities: The binomial model identifies the up and down factors as 1 plus (or minus, if the change is negative) the assumed percentage price change for each period: Each period's up and down factors depend on the underlying's presumed volatility (Choice C). For the binomial model, volatility is reflected only in how much the underlying can move up or down in one period. This influences not only the magnitude of the move, but also the risk-neutral probability of a move in either direction: In the binomial model, there are only two possible outcomes, so the probability of a down move equals 1 – the probability of an up move. If the risk-free rate is 5%, then the risk-neutral probability of an up move is [(1 + 0.05) − 0.80]/(1.20 − 0.80) = 0.625 or 62.5%, and the risk-neutral probability of a down move is 1 − 0.625 = 0.375, or 37.5%. (Choice B) The binomial model assumes an investor can construct a portfolio consisting of some amount of the underlying and one call option. This portfolio generates the same return whether the underlying goes up or down. Since this portfolio is risk-free, investors' risk preferences are irrelevant, so the model requires only the risk-neutral probability of an up or down move, not the actual probability.

subtopic: 9.01 Alternative Investment Features, Methods, and Structures
question_en: When co-investing, investors most likely:
option_a: rely heavily on the fund manager's due diligence.
option_b: source the investment idea and have others invest alongside.
option_c: raise additional capital to fund the investment once the investing decision has been made.
explanation_en: Co-investing in alternative investments Advantages Disadvantages Offers direct investing experience Requires more resources and expertise Leverages the investment firm's process than fund investing and expertise Direct investing opportunities are Reduced management fees dependent on the investment firm More active approach Potential adverse selection bias Coinvesting occurs when an investor in an alternative fund (eg, hedge fund, venture capital) accepts the opportunity to invest directly (ie, direct private investment outside the fund structure) by committing additional capital in specific investments alongside the fund manager who introduced the idea (ie, acted as an intermediary). Coinvesting requires two processes that demand more resources and expertise from the investor: fund-specific due diligence and asset-specific due diligence. Considerable asset-specific due diligence is performed by the investment firm (ie, general partner and fund manager) when it acts as an intermediary and presents the opportunity to the investor. Coinvesting is often a transitional step for investors to learn the details and fine points of direct investing. In addition, decisions to coinvest are often made under tight deadlines, putting considerable pressure on the investor to thoroughly complete the required level of due diligence. For these reasons, many investors rely heavily on the fund manager's due diligence expertise when evaluating a coinvestment opportunity. (Choice B) The investment firm, not the investor, sources the investment idea and has others invest alongside. (Choice C) Since the deadlines for decision-making and funding are usually tight, raising additional funding capital is not normally an option once the decision to coinvest has been made.

question_en: Compared with traditional investments, alternative investments are least likely to have:
explanation_en: Common characteristics of alternative investments compared with traditional investments Less liquid Less regulation Less transparency More active management Higher fee structure Higher minimum investments Less flexibility Alternative investments refer to vehicles established to invest both in traditional asset classes such as stocks and bonds as well as in nontraditional asset classes such as commodities and real estate. The term also refers to nontraditional investments, such as private equity funds and hedge funds. Alternative investments generally cater to institutions and wealthy individuals. In theory, these are sophisticated investors who can perform their own due diligence and oversight, which minimizes their need for regulatory protection. As a result, alternative investments are subject to fewer reporting requirements than are traditional investments. The level of reporting in alternative investments is far more likely to be cursory than detailed. (Choice A) Many alternative investment strategies employ large amounts of leverage (ie, borrowing) to enhance investment returns. Shorting a security is a form of leverage. Entering a short position means that the fund borrows an underlying security and sells it in anticipation that its price will fall and the company can buy the security back at a lower price in the future. (Choice C) Most types of alternative investments are characterized by active management. While traditional investments can also be actively managed, they typically use passive management more than alternative investments do.

question_en: Which of the following choices most likely describes a benefit of adding alternative investments to a portfolio of traditional investments?
explanation_en: Alternative investments refer to investments in nontraditional assets such as commodities, real estate, private equity, and hedge funds. The term also refers to vehicles, such as limited partnerships, created to invest in traditional asset classes (eg, stocks, bonds). Alternative investments are attractive since they give investors access to a broader range of assets classes and have the potential to provide diversification benefits when added to a traditional asset portfolio. Typically, alternative assets have lower correlations with traditional assets. (Choice A) The markets for these assets are typically less liquid (ie, assets cannot be sold as quickly for cash) than markets for traditional assets. As a result, adding alternative assets to a traditional asset portfolio most likely decreases the portfolio's liquidity. (Choice B) Alternative investments are subject to less regulation than traditional investments, which results in fewer reporting requirements and therefore less transparency. Alternative investments also have higher fee structures (eg, hedge funds have both management and incentive fees).

question_en: For a small firm, co-investing in alternative assets is most likely:
option_a: attractive as it avoids adverse-selection bias.
option_b: attractive due to the elimination of the intermediary.
option_c: challenging due to the resources and expertise needed.
explanation_en: The three most common methods of investing in alternative investments, ordered by increasing level of involvement or expertise required, are: Fund investing: The investor invests in a fund (eg, hedge, private equity) that makes all investment decisions. Fund investing is an indirect method of investing. Co-investing: An investor in an alternative fund (eg, venture, private equity) has the opportunity to invest directly (ie, private investment outside of the fund structure) by committing additional capital in specific investments along with the fund manager who introduced the idea (ie, acts as an intermediary). Direct investing: An investor makes a direct investment in an asset (eg, taking a position in a private company directly, without the use of an intermediary). Investing in any alternative investment requires due diligence. For a small firm, resources (eg, assets, firm capital) and expertise are most likely limited, which makes fund investing attractive as it requires the lowest level of involvement. Co-investing is challenging for a small firm: it requires two separate due diligence processes (ie, fund and asset-specific processes), demanding more resources and expertise. (Choices A and B) Co-investing does not eliminate the intermediary, as it is the fund's investment firm that is presenting the co-investment idea/opportunity to the investor. This dynamic introduces adverse-selection bias since the fund firm is incentivized to keep the best deals for themselves.

question_en: An investor is conducting due diligence on a hedge fund. Which of the following is most likely to be readily available? Information on the fund's:
explanation_en: Alternative investments (eg, private equity, venture capital, real estate) often have a waterfall distribution framework for paying out returns/profits. Generally, limited partners (ie, LP investors) receive distributions equal to their initial capital outlay plus profits up to the hurdle rate; the general partner (GP) is then paid a performance fee. At this point, unless the limited partnership agreement contains a catch-up clause, distributions and profits are split proportionately between the GP and LPs. Waterfall distribution methods are classified as either: deal-by-deal (American style) or whole-of-fund (European style). The timing of performance fee payments makes deal-by-deal waterfalls more advantageous to the GP since each deal is evaluated as each investment is exited. This allows the GP an opportunity to receive performance fee cash flows earlier (eg, annually) than under the whole-of-fund method. (Choice A) In deal-by-deal waterfalls, a clawback provision would likely be included in the partnership agreement to protect the LPs by restoring the profit split if subsequent investments in the portfolio do not earn performance fees. This provision "claws back" the performance fee already paid to the GP and is not to the GP's advantage. (Choice C) A whole-of-fund waterfall pays the GP based on the performance of the entire fund. This delays payment of performance fees until the end of the fund's life (eg, 7–8 years), which is not to the GP's advantage.

question_en: A hedge fund has a fee structure with a high-water mark but no hurdle rates. The high-water mark most likely:
option_a: resets with a new calendar year.
option_b: will not apply if a fund always has positive returns.
option_c: triggers fees from all fund investors at the same time.
explanation_en:
A high-water mark (HWM) is the highest value that a fund has previously achieved for a given investor in the fund. It is used as a threshold for
calculating whether that investor will owe the fund manager a performance fee (also called an incentive fee or carried interest).
HWMs ensure that performance fees are paid only when managers exceed prior HWMs, not when the fund recovers from previous losses. A
manager cannot receive a performance fee in subsequent periods unless the fund's value exceeds the existing HWM (ie, sets a new HWM). A
manager who can constantly increase the fund's value (and therefore constantly exceed prior HWMs) would always earn performance fees,
assuming the manager is not also required to meet hurdle rates.
(Choice A) A HWM does not reset with a new calendar year; it resets when the fund reaches a new high value.
(Choice C) HWMs vary by investor (also known as a limited partner [LP]), depending on the fund's value when the LP invested. Therefore, an
investor may or may not pay a performance fee at any given time, depending on whether the manager has exceeded that investor's HWM.

manager. Funds also tend to have lower minimum capital requirements than co-investment or direct investment opportunities.

question_en: A clawback provision protects the limited partner from excess fees paid to the general partner in a private equity fund. Which of the following situations most likely activates a clawback provision?
option_a: Committed capital was never fully drawn down
option_b: Profits and incentive fees were distributed annually
option_c: Management fees are forfeited due to poor performance
explanation_en:
Clawback provision
Limited partners are due their initial investment plus 80% of fund profits
Clawback is triggered to restore the 80/20 profit split balance
Requires the general partner to return incentive fees to the limited partners
Occurs when fees are paid over time instead of at wind down of a private equity fund
Private equity funds charge both an annual management fee and an incentive fee. The typical structure pays the general partner (GP) a 2%
management fee and 20% of profits (ie, 2 and 20).
The management fee is initially based on committed capital and converts only to assets under management (AUM) when the commitment period
ends or when all funds are drawn down. During the commitment period (eg, 3 years), investors are contractually obligated to provide cash (up to
their commitment level) when demanded by the fund. Investors do not actually provide capital until the fund needs cash for an investment.
The incentive fee is based on realized profits from the sale of the fund's investments. If incentive fees are paid throughout the life of the fund as
investments are sold, a situation could occur where losses or small gains on other holdings result in the GP receiving more than 20% of the
profits. In this situation, the clawback provision requires the GP to repay a portion of the incentive fee or to forfeit future incentive fees to
restore the 80/20 profit split balance.
(Choices A and C) Management fees are initially based on committed capital and convert to AUM when the commitment period ends; however,
the clawback provision applies only to incentive fees, regardless of fund performance.
